utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could Mr. Registrar call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, case number IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Can we have the appearances for the Prosecution, please, though we know one another very well by now.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, good morning, Your Honours. For the Prosecution, myself, Daryl Mundis, and myself, Tecla Benjamin, and the case manager, Ruth Karper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Madam Benjamin. And now the attorneys that we know very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of General Hadzihasanovic: Edina Residovic, counsel; Stephane Bourgon, co-counsel; and Mirna Milanovic, the legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have the appearances for the other Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Kubura, Rodney Dixon, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, and Mr. Mulalic, the legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The Chamber wishes to greet all those present, representatives of the Prosecution, Defence, as well as all the staff in this courtroom. We have on the programme for today two witnesses. Madam Benjamin or Mr. Mundis, could you tell us the order in which your witnesses will be appearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. The first witness will be Ivan Bohutinski. The second witness is as scheduled, and the Prosecution will be making an application for protective measures with respect to that witness. Mr. President, also, if I may, while I'm on my feet, as Your Honours are well aware, today was the deadline for the Prosecution to file its further observations, if any, with respect to the Defence motion for judicial notice of adjudicated facts. The Prosecution would respectfully request an extension in order to file those observations. We would ask that they be -- that we be given until Tuesday, 23 March, that is, next Tuesday, in order to -- to file our observations. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will grant you this extension of time, until Tuesday, the 23rd of March. Would Madam Usher be kind enough to go and bring in the first witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the President, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me check that you are hearing in your own language what I am saying to you. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have been called to appear as a witness by the Prosecution. Before asking you to read the solemn declaration, I would like you to tell me your first and last name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Ivan Bohutinski.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When were you born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 25th of June, 1973.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 25th of June, 1973. And where were you born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Zenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I completed a school for auto mechanics, and I'm now working in a company as a driver.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't have the translation of what you were saying. I have the English transcript. I am not hearing the interpreter in French.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's okay now. I can hear the interpreter. You told us that you are now a driver in a company. In 1993, what were you doing at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1993, ten years ago, what were you engaged in? Did you have a job? What were you doing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I wasn't working. I was still going to school. I was completing my studies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Have you already testified in court, or is this the first time for you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please read the solemn declaration that I am giving you through the intermediary of Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before giving the floor to representatives of the Prosecution, I should like to give you some information regarding the proceedings in this court. You will be answering questions that will be put to you in a moment by representatives of the Prosecution, on your right. After that stage, which will last a certain amount of time, the lawyers representing the accused, who are to your left, will also have questions for you. The three Judges, who are in front of you, may also, if they find it necessary, at any point in time ask you questions. Sometimes the question may be complicated. And if you don't understand the meaning, please ask the person who is asking you the question to rephrase it. Before answering, think over your answer and try to give a full and precise answer, because as we have no written documents, what you tell us will be used to establish the truth. Therefore, your testimony is important and your replies also need to be complete and precise. There are also two minor provisions that I wish to refer to, and that is: Since you have solemnly declared to tell the truth, you cannot provide false testimony. Should you do that, you could be prosecuted, as anyone who provides false testimony, and this may be punished by a penalty under prison sentence or both. Also, there's another provision in the Rules which envisages that when a witness is answering a question, if that answer may possibly incriminate him, that could lead to subsequent prosecution against him, he can refuse to answer. Should that happen, the Chamber can compel him to answer nevertheless, but in that case he is protected because what he says cannot be used as evidence against him in the future. I needed to provide those explanations, as the procedure may not be quite clear for you, and with a view to ensuring smooth proceedings. So I thought it necessary to give you these explanations. Without further ado, as we have another witness after you, I give the floor now to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. Bohutinski, you indicated to the Trial Chamber that you were born in Zenica. Could you say the municipality in which Zenica is Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. located.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: Zenica is a municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us the breakdown of the -- the ethnic breakdown of your fellow villagers in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: I don't know the percentages, but as far as I know, Muslims live there. There are some Croats and some Serbs, but not many.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters can barely hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Witness, could you speak up a little louder, please.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: As far as I know, Zenica is inhabited by Muslims. There are some Croats and some Serbs, but very few. I am not familiar with the percentages.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Did there come a time when you were enlisted for any military service? Could you assist us, please.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: Yes. I was called up to serve in the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And could you tell us the period for which you served.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: I didn't serve in the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Could you tell us what you did.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: What I did? I was supposed to go and serve in the JNA, but I refused to do that and I moved to Croatia, because I have a house there, and I went there to avoid going to the JNA. So I moved to Croatia, and I spent some time over there.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Now, at the commencement of January 1993, where were you living at that time?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: Could you just tell me -- oh, I see it on the screen. Could you just tell me which month you mean. January? At the beginning --

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: At the commencement of January 1993.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: I was living in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you moved back to Zenica?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: It was like this: I returned from Croatia to Busovaca. I'm not an inhabitant of Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you. State for the Trial Chamber, please, Mr. Bohutinski, what was the atmosphere in Busovaca at the time in January 1993.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: Well, you see, it was tense, up until the second half. And in the second half of January, I think it was precisely on the 25th of January, conflicts broke out between the Croats and the Bosniaks, or Muslims. Fighting started on the 25th early in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: How old were you at this time, Mr. Bohutinski?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: I was 19.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And at this time, you were still not a member of any army, were you?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: I was attending training. Twenty days prior to that at the barracks in Busovaca, training in the army of the HVO, the Croatian Defence Council. I underwent training, but this was quite insignificant.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Could you state for the Trial Chamber what transpired on the morning of the 25th of January, when the conflict began.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: According to what I understood, the war broke out between the Muslims and Croats in the territory of Busovaca municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Where were you on the 25th of January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: I was in my home in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: What did you hear? Tell us what happened on that morning.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: In the morning, when we got up, we heard rifle shots and shots from automatic rifles and machine-guns, shooting.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Did you go to see where the shooting was coming from?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: Judging by the sound of the shots, I was able to judge that this was coming from above my house, because I live in a part of the town close to a hill. So behind my house was the slope and the hill, and they were shooting from there.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Could you explain for the Trial Chamber whom you mean when you say "they were shooting."

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: I didn't know at first who it was that was shooting, and then later, looking through the window, I saw HVO soldiers going along the road and passing to the left of my house. Since I saw it was the HVO, I knew that the Muslims were behind my house and that they were the ones who had opened fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Did there come a time - excuse me - during the day when you had to leave your house?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Where did you go to?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: I drove my father to hospital, because he had been wounded.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: What was he wounded by?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: With an automatic rifle.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Did he wound himself?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: He didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Could you explain for us -- could you explain to the Trial Chamber how he got wounded, please.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: As the HVO had come from the left side of my house, a couple of hundred metres away, they didn't know, as my house is in a part of the town that is inhabited exclusively by Muslims - ours was the only Croat house in that part of town - and as they didn't know who we were and that this was our house, as the Muslims were shooting from the houses, they were mopping up that part of the town. And as we entered a room where he was wounded - I don't remember exactly whether it was me or one of my sisters or mother - moved the curtain, and they noticed this, and they thought that perhaps we were going to open fire, as they didn't know who we were, so they opened fire on our house. And the bullet flew in through the window and wounded my father.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: So would it be correct in saying that your father got wounded in the process of the conflict, when it just started? Would it be correct in saying that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Okay. Did there come a time when you enlisted in the -- in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: No. I couldn't join the JNA, because the war had already started.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you were drafted in the JNA, after the war?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: [Inaudible response]

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Did you ever do service with the JNA?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: No. I was just recruited for a medical examination, but I never joined. I never went.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Specifically with respect to Easter of 1993, where were you at that time?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: At Easter, I was on the front line, the separation line between -- in Donje Milavice.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And with whom were you in the front line, which unit?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: The Croatian Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Did you remain on the front line?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you surrendered?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Tell the Trial Chamber what took place after you surrendered.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: We were captured by Muslim forces, and they killed one of my colleagues and wounded another, and then they transferred us to the school in the village of Lugovi - that is, the Muslim forces - the school at Lugovi, where we spent, shall we say, an hour or two. And then they handed us over to the 333rd Brigade of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the brigade from Kacuni, in Kacuni, which is a village near Busovaca. They handed us over, I suppose it was some sort of a police. I don't know whether they were military or civilian police. Then they shut us up in a room there and we waited.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: During the time you were in Kacuni, could you tell us what happened.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: I was in the prison in the silo at Kacuni. They interrogated us. We were imprisoned there. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And could you give the Trial Chamber an idea of what the interrogation consisted of.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: As all the Muslims in Kacuni knew me and I knew them, so they didn't question me much, just some small details. They asked me about my father, who had killed the father of a Muslim, Krompiras. They asked me whether I knew who had killed him in Busovaca, and things like that. They didn't ask me too much. For instance, they asked me where Kordic was accommodated and Sliskovic and where the military police was, where the civilian police was, things like that. Those were the questions I was asked.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: For how long did you remain at the silos?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, but between seven and ten days, because this was a long time ago and I don't remember too well.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us -- could you give us an idea of the physical conditions and how you were treated at the silo.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: No one hurt me in the silo, but two of my colleagues, who were with me in prison, who were captured when I was taken out of prison -- when I returned, they had been beaten up. They were covered in blood and in a very poor state.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: What were the physical conditions like in the silo?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: Very bad. It was cold. We didn't have any beds. We slept on the floor, on some blankets. There was no furnace to heat the room.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. -- Sir, could you wait for a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think that the questions being put by my learned friend are not included in any of the counts of the indictment, the silo or any other points that are being referred to now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was something that occurred to me too, Mrs. Benjamin. He tells us that he was detained in this silo for seven days in the village of Kacuni, and this is not included in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, I do agree, but I needed to -- to get to a certain point, and so I just introduced that. In fact, the Prosecution had no intention on staying long on it, by all means. But he needed to get from there to another place that is in -- it's in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: In light of what has just been said, could you tell us from the silo if you were taken anywhere.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And were you taken to another detention centre?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: No. I was released. I was free.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: After you were released, were you picked up again and taken anywhere?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Kindly tell the Trial Chamber where you were taken, please.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: I was freed in Zenica. I stayed with an aunt there. And from that apartment, I was taken in to the 303rd Brigade in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Could you tell the Trial Chamber where in Zenica you were taken to.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: They took me to the mechanical engineering faculty, where their headquarters was.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And are you able to tell the Court what part of the faculty you were taken to?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: In a room that was perhaps 15 square metres in size. I went in.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And could you tell us when you got there, your experience, please.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: They opened the door and told me to go inside and sit down. Inside there was someone like a policeman wearing a military uniform. He told me to sit down. I sat down. And he told me that I mustn't turn my head around, that I must look straight at him, that somebody was going to open the door to see me and that I mustn't turned around. And just then the door opened, and I heard a female voice, and the policeman sitting in front of me asked this woman whether she knew me, and she said yes. After that, a couple of minutes later, he started questioning me about things in Busovaca, where the military police was, where their command was, where the civilian police was, where Dario Kordic was. He also asked me about Krompiras's father, who had killed him. I don't know. I couldn't answer, because I didn't know. And then he said that I did know but that I didn't want to tell him and that he could make me tell him.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: At the end of your interrogation, where were you taken to?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: I was released. They let me go back to my flat.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: You were released from the room in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. They allowed me to return to my flat in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And what did --

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: They transferred me there from Kacuni.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And what did you do in your flat in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: I was at my aunt's. My mother's aunt was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. Bohutinski, after you left your aunt's flat, you indicated to the Trial Chamber that you were taken to a room in Zenica. Are we on the same page?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: So I'm asking you now to tell the Trial Chamber when you were taken to that room what transpired. First tell us what part of the building was the room.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: We went in. And after the entrance, I think it was the first room on the right. It was a small room. There was nothing in there, just a table. In fact, I've told you what happened in the room.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Okay. So after you were interrogated in that room, were you taken anywhere in that building?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Were you ever kept in that building for any length of time?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: Not for very long. Perhaps an hour, roughly speaking. I don't know how long I spent there exactly, but about one hour.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Well, tell the Trial Chamber what happened after.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: They then released me, and then I returned to my aunt's flat in Zenica. I spent the afternoon there. I slept over. And then on the following day - I don't know at what time - someone knocked on the door.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And did you go anywhere?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: Yes. We opened the door. In fact, my aunt opened the door, and there were some policemen standing in front of the door.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And could you tell the Trial Chamber what happened.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's fine now. When my aunt opened the door, there were some policemen standing in front of the door. They asked whether Ivan Bohutinski was there in her flat, and she said yes. They asked me to go out. I went out, and they told me to go with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And did you go with them?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Okay. Explain to the Trial Chamber who you mean when you say "them" and describe what they looked like to you.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: The policemen. When I said "them," I was referring to the policemen, policemen from the 7th Muslim Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Were they wearing uniforms?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: Yes, they were wearing military uniforms. They had white belts and that's why I assumed that they were military policemen. They had patches on their arms, on their right arms.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Were you taken to any particular place?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: I went with them. We got into a car. I didn't know where I was going until I arrived there. I arrived at the music school in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: So you were taken to the Zenica Music School. Could you tell us, when you got to the Zenica Music School, what happened, if anything? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: They took me into a room in which there was a television set. They were probably having breakfast or lunch. In fact, that was a room where people would have lunch.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Did anything happen in the room, Mr. Bohutinski?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: I spent several hours there. In the meantime, a young man - I don't know who - arrived in a shirt covered in blood. He entered the room and he took a container with food from the room and he went off with it somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Could you tell the Trial Chamber in relation to you what took place in the room.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: I spent several hours there. No one asked me about anything. No one said anything to me. I watched television for a while. It was on. I thought that I was waiting for someone.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Did there come a time eventually when someone came?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: Yes. In the early evening hours, perhaps. I couldn't tell you when exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And could you tell the Trial Chamber what happened then.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: The policeman took me to a floor in the building and he took me into a dark room, where I saw a man sitting in an armchair. He had a rifle in his lap. He had a slight beard, longish hair. He told me to sit down, which I did. And he said that he had brought me up to be a good child, that he had taught me to be a good child, but that I turned out to be an insolent person and this is why I had been captured and brought to see him. I recognised the person. He was a teacher of ours from Busovaca. His name was Jasmin Isic.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Could you tell the Trial Chamber where this room was located. Was this at the top floor? Where was the room located?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: Well, I really can't remember, but I wouldn't say that it was on the last floor. This happened a long time ago, so I can't remember. All I know is that the room was dark.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Could you tell the Trial Chamber now or relate for the Trial Chamber a typical day in the life of that room for you. What happened? What did you see? What did you do, if anything?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: You mean the day I spent with Jasmin Isic, in that room?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: I was in the room. He gave me a pen and paper. He asked me where Kordic and Sliskovic were. I said I didn't know. He asked me who Krompiras's father was. He asked me to tell him who had expelled so many people. I said I didn't know. He then produced a sheet of white paper, a blank sheet of paper and a pen. He told me to write something down. I didn't know what to write down, because I had no information. I didn't know where these locations were in Busovaca. He then gave me a sheet of paper and started shouting at me. He started shouting at me. He started cursing me. And then a policeman entered the room and told him to take me away and to beat me up.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Were you -- witness, may I interrupt. Were you eventually taken away from that room?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Tell the Trial Chamber where you were taken to.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: They took me to the prison, to the basement. That was cabinet number 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Describe for the Trial Chamber the room that you're referring to that they said they took you to in the basement. Could you describe what you saw when you got there, how the room looked, if there was anybody in the room. Could you please tell us.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: Well, when I got there, I saw there were about 15 people in the room -- let's say about 15. I didn't know what the exact number was. All of them -- almost all of them had been maltreated, beaten. They were covered in blood. No medical assistance had been provided for them. No one helped them. One person wasn't even able to walk. He had some sort of kidney problems. That's what he told me. I asked him about that. I asked him what they were doing there. They said that they had been detained, that they had been beaten in the prison. They said that no one knew that they were in the prison. It was a dark room. The windows were covered with some sort of sandbags. We didn't have any facilities. For sleeping, there were some sort of pallets on the floor. In the corner, there were two tables that had been put together. There was some sort of sponge on them, but it wasn't possible to sleep on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: What were your hygienic conditions like? Did you have a toilet? Did you bathe? What were the conditions like?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: The hygienic conditions were non-existent. If we wanted to relieve ourselves, we had to call the policeman on duty. We'd go up and outside. To urinate, we had a 10-litre container in the corner. That's what we used to urinate in. We didn't have any water. We didn't have any drinking water. We'd have to go outside to get drinking water. There was no bathroom down there.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Now, for how long did you stay at this room in the basement in the Zenica Music School?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: I can't tell you how long exactly, but on the 18th -- on the 18th of May, I got out of the prison. So it was perhaps the 27th or 28th or 29th of April, up until the 18th of May.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, tell me, during that period of time that you spent at -- in the basement of the Zenica Music School, what was life like for you? How was -- how was -- describe a routine day. What happened?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: Living conditions down there were very difficult. The conditions were really bad. Life was very difficult for me and for my comrades who were down there. But if you want me to describe a particular day for you, I'll do so. Just tell me --

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Yes, you can. Any particular day that you think is of significance to you, could you describe it for the Trial Chamber, please.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: Well, for example, when I went to clean in the music school, a military policeman came to fetch me in the prison. He called my name out. When I approached the bars at the exit, he told me that he was from Busovaca. He said that no one would touch me and he said that I should go and clean their rooms. I agreed to do so. The man took me out and up the stairs, up to the top of the building. He gave me a broom and a bucket full of water, I think, and he told me that I should go and clean up. I followed him. He asked me how things were in Busovaca. I wasn't provoked. We got into a room on the floor. He told me to take my shoes off and to go into the room and clean it. I opened the door, entered the room, and I saw that this was a room where the Muslims would perform their religious rites. There were rugs on the floor and they would probably kneel down on them.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. Bohutinski, so one -- are you saying to the Trial Chamber that one of your duties while you were there was to clean the rooms? Am I right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: I only cleaned the rooms on one occasion.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: I don't know what they thought about these duties.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Tell the Trial Chamber, did any other activities take place? Were you subjected to interrogation? Could you please explain to us what happened during your days.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: Well, when I was in the cell down there, a couple of policemen would appear. I don't know their names. And they asked me to give them money so that they could exchange me, to release me. They asked me whether I was Ivcan Bilic's grandson. They asked me whether my grandfather had any money, and they said they could arrange this exchange but that I had to pay for it, and they wanted to know roughly how much my grandfather could pay for this exchange.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. Bohutinski, very briefly but precisely tell the Trial Chamber, did you give anybody any money?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Were you eventually exchanged?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: When you were in the basement or during your period of -- of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. imprisonment in the basement, did you hear anything at all besides, I mean, seeing what you saw, what you told us? Did you hear anything from the basement?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: I heard them beating in a room. I didn't see the beatings, but you could hear people groaning. I realised that they were beating someone in that room upstairs to the right of the entrance. That's where the soldiers probably had their dormitory. I heard them beating someone.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And for how long would you say that these beatings went on for?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: I don't know. For up to about half an hour. I don't believe it went on for any longer than that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you. And when you were exchanged at the music school, where did you go to?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: I went to Vitez. I was exchanged. I went to Vitez. I then returned from Vitez. I only spent one day there. And then I returned to my place of birth, to Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. Bohutinski, state for the trial opinion -- state for the Trial Chamber what is your opinion of what transpired on -- from January 1993 until April 1993. How do you feel about what happened?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: Well, very briefly and concisely, if you watch a horror film at night and then go to sleep, would you be able to sleep well? It was chaos. The situation was very difficult. It was difficult to survive in such a situation and remain a normal person. It was really intolerable.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, this is the examination-in-chief of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'll now turn to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Bohutinski. My name is Edina Residovic. I represent General Hadzihasanovic. I would like you to answer a number of questions. And if there is a question that you don't understand, please let me know. In response to a question put to you by the Prosecution, you said that you were born in Zenica but that you grew up in Busovaca; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: After you had been summoned to be recruited into the JNA, you avoided responding because war had already broken out in the Republic of Croatia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you returned to Bosnia and Herzegovina, the JNA attacked Bosnia-Herzegovina soon after; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Although you were of age, you didn't report to the HVO or to the Territorial Defence immediately, although these organisations existed in Busovaca at the time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, after going through training, the HVO requested that you join their units, which you did at the beginning of 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In response to a question put to you by my learned colleague, you said that the tension in Busovaca between the HVO and the Territorial Defence at the time started at the beginning of 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, the armed conflict, as you have stated, started on the 25th of January; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You lived with your family in a part of Busovaca which was inhabited by mostly Muslim -- Muslims and Bosniaks; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In that part of Busovaca, you were in fact the only Croatian family; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your relationships and your parents' relationships with your neighbours had always been good; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: On that day, on the 25th of January, it was clear to you, given the shooting from all sides, that an armed conflict had started in Busovaca between the units of the BH army and the units of the HVO; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At that point in time, you didn't know who had started the conflict; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, as you have already said, you saw HVO members approaching your house.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You also noticed that the HVO was shooting at each house, because they knew that that part of town was inhabited by Bosniaks; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: By mistake, since they weren't aware of the fact that you were a Croatian family, they also shot at your house; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your father was wounded with dumdum bullets, fragmentation bullets.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Those fragmentation bullets were fired at your house by someone from HVO positions. This person thought that the house was inhabited by Bosniaks. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: Yes, most likely.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: After you'd taken your father to hospital, you found out that the HVO had captured all army members by the end of the day and took them and a large part of the population to the Kaonik prison.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: I didn't know about the Kaonik prison. I didn't have that information.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, you were aware of the fact that they had been captured and taken away; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: After these conflicts, the HVO took full control of Busovaca and virtually all the Bosniak population of Busovaca was expelled.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: Not all, but most of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You joined the HVO in mid-April 1993; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: Yes, on the 16th.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very soon after that, while you were on the HVO front lines, another armed conflict started against the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In answer to a question from my learned friend, you said that after the killing of one of your colleagues, a member of the HVO, and the wounding of another, you surrendered; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You were taken to the command post of the 303rd Brigade of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Actually, as you said, it was the so-called Kacuni Brigade. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: One of the commanders present was Alija Begic, whom you knew; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: During the interrogation, you realised that they were asking for military information.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: During that interrogation and the following days, while you were in detention of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, people treated you Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. correctly. No one mistreated you.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: No, no one beat me, but I didn't have normal conditions in those places of detention.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Five or six days later you were released, and you yourself chose to go to Zenica, because they asked you whether you had anyone in Visoko or somewhere else; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: I was supposed to go to Busovaca first, but it wasn't possible to go there, to pass. And then they asked me whether I had someone in Visoko or Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Commander Begic wanted to release you to go home but the combat conditions did not allow it; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So then you decided to stay with your aunt, and they transported you safely to Zenica; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: While you were staying at the music school, you personally were not physically mistreated once; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The only incorrect point was when these unknown soldiers demanded money from you for exchange.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: Unknown soldiers and also Jasmin Isic, because he -- him, I knew, and he also asked me for money for the exchange.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bohutinski, you are now living in correct and, one might say, friendly relations with most of the Bosniaks who are living in Busovaca or in the environs, and you know them; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The other Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. On behalf of Mr. Kubura's Defence team, I have a few questions for today's witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bohutinski, you described earlier on today during your testimony that you were captured on the 19th of March, 1993, just before Easter; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: Yes. The 19th of March?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: The 19th of April. I'm sorry. At the time, you were captured as a member of the HVO; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: Yes, on the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: You surrendered or, rather, you were captured by a unit known as the Black Swans; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: After interrogation in the 303rd Brigade, you went to Zenica, as you just told my colleague, Madam Residovic.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: On the 29th of April, 1993, you went to the music school.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: I can't confirm the exact date. It was a long time ago. Now, whether it was exactly then, but around that date.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Very shortly after your arrival at the music school, you met Isic Jasmin; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Jasmin Isic was someone you knew before the war; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Jasmin Isic was a person of doubtful character. Before the war, he was prone to gambling, stealing; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: You described your first conversation with Jasmin Isic. Is it true that he ordered that no one may beat you?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: He repeated that several times.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: When you went to the basement the first time, you found 15 persons down there.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: They were mostly members of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: Yes, I think, but there were civilians too, because they were coming in civilian clothes. Yes, I think there were civilians too. Not just members of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: You know the name Krunoslav Rajic?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: He was in the music school at the same time as you were.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Krunoslav Rajic is also a person who was not physically mistreated in any way.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: While I was there, he wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: During your stay at the music school, some members of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina were brought there too; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: During your stay, you had occasion to be visited by medical personnel or, rather, nurses on behalf of the army and the 7th Muslim Brigade.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: Just once, because I complained I had stomach pain. And then they sent me a nurse with a green bag who gave me some pills. And this was just for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: You were also visited by your aunt from Zenica; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: No. She came to visit me, but they wouldn't let her see me. But when the exchange took place, she came.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: They allowed her to leave you food and clothes to change into; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Contact was established with you very shortly through these soldiers, who said that a certain amount of money was required for you exchange.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: This offer was repeated to you personally by Jasmin Isic.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: Only a smaller sum was suggested than the one demanded by the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: And those soldiers were speaking on behalf of Jasmin Isic?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: I don't know that. No one said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: The first sum mentioned was the sum of 50.000 German marks; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: Yes, a fair-haired policeman asked me for that amount.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: You were allowed to contact your father by phone; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: Yes, but later.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: You passed on this sum to your father.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: You know that Jasmin Isic spoke to your uncle regarding the exchange and the money requested.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: And your uncle's name is Janko Batinic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Regarding the negotiations, if we can call them that, about your exchange, you met Mr. Karalic [Realtime transcript read in error "Krljaca"] in the music school as well.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: Not directly. But the people in the prison told me that that was his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Your father told you that he could only raise 10.000 German marks for your exchange.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: At the end, an agreement was reached that that would be -- that the price would be 7.000 German marks.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: Yes, and that they had to be deposited on an account for Muslim refugees from Busovaca. I don't really know what he meant when he said that. That is what Jasmin said to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Jasmin Isic was dissatisfied with this price, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: On the 18th of May, you left the music school.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Throughout your stay there, from about the 29th of April until the 18th of May, you were not mistreated in any way or beaten in the music school.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: The only duty you had during your stay there was the cleaning that you described. You had no other duties or work to do.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: No, we didn't do anything. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We have no further questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Madam Benjamin, have you any re-examination for this witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: I just have one question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. Bohutinski, at the basement of the Zenica Music School, did you get three regular meals per day?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: Sometimes we didn't. And when we did get meals, they were very bad meals that we were not satisfied with. The food was insufficient. When I went to prison and when I returned, I had lost between 10 and 12 kilograms, which shows that the food was nowhere near adequate.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And in your opinion, you were treated correctly in the basement?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: Well, I really don't know what to say. I don't know what exactly you mean, whether they treated me correctly or not. They didn't touch me. But the very fact that I was there in the basement is a bad thing, which shows that they didn't treat me well. Had they treated me well, they would have let me go free.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, this concludes this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. For the transcript, on page 30, line 8, the name is misspelt. It should be Karalic and not Krljaca.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The transcript will be corrected accordingly so that the names are spelt properly. Thank you, sir, for coming to testify. You have answered the questions of the Prosecution and of the Defence. Thank you for having contributed to the establishment of the truth for you testimony. We wish you a safe journey home. And the usher will be kind enough to escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us now go into private session, as the Prosecution has an application to make for protective measures.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Carry on, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: You earlier mentioned that the attacks on the area of responsibility were carried out by units of the 7th Muslim Brigade, the 328th Brigade, the 306th Brigade, and the 314th Brigade. Can you say which corps these units belonged to?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: Those units were part of the 3rd Corps of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Witness, can you recall - and I'd like you to listen to me very carefully, because we are moving on to a different corps - can you recall when the 7th Corps was formed? I am very sorry. I'll repeat the question. Witness, I'd like to ask you about another corps, the 7th Corps. Can you recall when the 7th Corps was formed?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: No, I can't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Very well. Can you remember the year?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: I think it was in 1993 or in 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Would the 7th Corps have been formed --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness has already said which units or corps participated. In the last three questions, the Prosecution is suggesting that the witness provide a different kind of answer, and we do not think that this is appropriate when conducting an examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. President, there is -- with respect --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Stamp, please take note of what has just been said. According to the common-law system, when a question is asked and the answer is precise, you are not allowed to ask the same question in order to obtain a different answer. You asked whether the witness could say -- if he could say when the 7th Corps was established. He said he couldn't. And that's the end of the matter. He can't tell you about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: With respect, Mr. President. He did not say he couldn't. He said he couldn't remember exactly, which is quite a different thing. So, therefore, the next question was: Can you remember the year? Which is not an improper question, having regard to the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But he wasn't able to answer the question. That's why the Defence intervened. Mrs. Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May I -- with respect to my friend, before she rises, there is --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness has just said that it could have been in 1993 or 1994. And in response to the previous questions before the discussion about the map, he said which corps participated in the attack on -- in this area before the 8th of June. So the witness has answered this question in several ways, and asking the witness any additional questions might lead the witness to provide a different sort of answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: With respect, Mr. President, the Prosecution is entitled to ask the witness questions of clarification or questions that will help him to give more precise evidence that will assist the Court in its deliberations. I respectfully submit that none of these questions I have asked is improper. What I think is -- well, I will not go as strongly as to say what I think is improper. May I just say that having regard to where we are, counsel and I know what the evidence is and understand the difficulties in terms of what has been said. Therefore, I should say for the record that it might well be proper in making some objections to do so outside of the hearing of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This point has already been raised by the Defence. Could you tell me what the question is in relation to the transcript, the question that you want to ask the witness in order to obtain clarifications? Because we would like to know what the question you want to put to the witness is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could the witness be taken out of hearing. It might well be -- it might not assist the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you like, that is not a problem. Madam Usher, could you escort the witness out of the courtroom. We'll lose ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stamp, please proceed and try and tell us about the question that you want to ask the witness. It seems that there is some confusion. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The witness earlier in chief said that among those involved in the offensive of the 8th of June was a battalion of the 7th Corps. The Prosecution is entitled to clarify that matter with a view to present before the Court the most accurate evidence that this witness is capable of giving, and that is just to assist the Court in its deliberations. The question to the witness -- the next question to the witness was whether or not he can recall whether the 7th Corps existed before the 8th of June or after the 8th of June. Because if it was created after the 8th of June, then certain obvious and logical inferences can be drawn in respect to that aspect of the testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'll listen to what the Defence has to say. But first of all, I would like to summarise the problem. In response to a question put to the witness, the witness said that the 7th Corps participated in the attack. The Prosecution wanted the witness to say -- to determine whether it was in fact the 7th Corps. They wanted to -- the witness to say when the 7th Corps was established. The witness was not able to answer the question, and as a result the Prosecution wanted the witness to inform them of the year in which the 7th Corps was established, in order to establish whether it could have been the 7th Corps on the 8th of June or whether it was the 3rd Corps. So this is what is at stake. What would the Defence like to say about the matter?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we have already expressed our position. This amounts to leading the witness. The Prosecution is trying to obtain the answer that they want from the witness. Naturally, the witness has been presented to the Trial Chamber as a military expert. This problem concerns the existence of a corps, the largest formation in the BH army, and the Prosecution wants to make it impossible for the Defence, in relation to the answer provided on page 47, line 23 and also answers provided when answering other questions. The witness quite clearly said that it could have been 1993 or 1994, so the witness [as interpreted] is trying to lead the witness in order to obtain the answer that they require and they want to prevent the Defence from asking questions on the basis of the answers that the witness provided before the Trial Chamber. We don't think that this is permissible, because the witness has answered the question to the best of his ability. We think that perhaps the Prosecution doesn't like the answer provided. But we think that the witness has already answered this question on three occasions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We will withdraw again to deliberate. --- Break taken at 12.24 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With regard to the problem raised, the Trial Chamber believes that the witness should clarify his answer, because the Trial Chamber doesn't exclude the possibility that the witness made a mistake with regard to the fact that the 7th Corps was in question. Perhaps he wanted to say that the 7th Brigade was in question. Either there was a translation error or the witness made a mistake. The 7th Corps was mentioned, but perhaps the witness was thinking of the 7th Brigade. As a result, the Trial Chamber will ask the witness to clarify the matter. Could the usher lower the blinds again and bring the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But before you take the floor, the Trial Chamber would like to ask the witness a question in order to clarify something. We are in open session, so we can ask the witness this question: In the course of the examination-in-chief, a question was put to you. You were asked who participated in the attack, and you said -- you informed us of the identity of those who participated in the attack, and you yourself said you were a member of the HVO. What we would like to know, because this is the subject of debate and perhaps it's the result of a translation error or perhaps you made a mistake when answering the question -- what we would like to know is the following: Who participated in the attack against the HVO? Could you tell us precisely. As you know, there are units within an army, units that consist of corps and units that we call brigades. Corps should not be confused with brigades. So the question that the Trial Chamber would like to ask you is the question that the Prosecution has already asked you, but the answer is problematic in that it is difficult to understand. My question is: Who participated in the attack against the HVO? Could you answer that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I testified on the basis of the intelligence that I had. According to the information I had, units of the BH 3rd Corps carried out the attack.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you say that these were units of the 3rd Corps. You did say "the 3rd Corps."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to the information that you were provided with, were there any other army corps or only 3rd Corps units? The question is precise.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the basis of what I experienced and what I have indicated on the map, when we were surrounded in the place called Ceke, I think a megaphone was probably used -- I know that they asked us to surrender, and the person who asked us to surrender said that he was from the BH army in Visoko. He said, "Surrender your weapons and we guarantee that the civilians will be safe."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the person who told you to do that, he was a member of which army corps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think that that brigade was part of the 1st Corps. It's really difficult to know what the exact structure in the army was, but I know that they asked us to surrender. I remember that well. And they said that it was the BH army from Visoko. As to whether that was true or not, I really could not say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But you can see that there is a problem. You said that you were surrounded by the 3rd Corps and those who asked you to surrender said that they were part of the 1st Corps. So it's necessary to know who was surrounding you. Was it the BH army that consisted of a number of corps or was it just the 3rd Corps or was it the 3rd Corps and the 1st Corps or a number of other corps? As far as you know, on the basis of the information that you had, who carried out the attack and which army corps attacked you and asked you to surrender?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, according to the information that I had, according to the intelligence I had, these were units from the 3rd Corps, and probably a brigade from Visoko. But I'm not sure of -- of the level of this formation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The answer is precise. The witness said it was the army's 3rd Corps and said that it was a unit - a brigade, not a corps - a brigade from Visoko. I think that this is clear. And the 7th Corps is not an issue that seems to arise. In order to be quite sure, did you have any information according to which the 7th Corps was also present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't know whether the 7th Corps had been established at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Stamp, you may continue. It was necessary to clarify the matter. I realised that there was a problem at the very beginning, but I wanted to allow the Prosecution to continue with its examination. Because on page 47, line 23 the problem that we have been debating for 20 minutes appeared.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you very much for the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have another five or, shall we say, ten minutes before the break, because there were several interruptions of the hearing. So let's say you have another ten minutes and then we'll have the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'm quite sure that I will not even use that amount of time.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Where was this -- you said probably there was a brigade from Visoko.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: We were at positions round the village of Ceke at the time. And members of that brigade were at the open cast mine area, a part of Strmac.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: From the information that you had, do you know whether or not members of that brigade from Visoko operated at any other position, apart from the open cast mine?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: I am really unable to answer that question. It was only from that direction that calls came for us to surrender.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Can you remember any of the names of the commanders of the brigades that were involved in the attack?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in open session now. Do you wish us to go into private session? We are in open session now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Just, if you can, just tell us the names based on the information you have of persons who were in leadership positions in the brigades involved in the attack at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: So as you have already said, on the 8th of June an intensified attack was directed against these defence lines of yours in Mrkonje; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: You were able to hear both artillery and infantry fire in the attack.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: Yes. I even heard cries of "Tekbir, Allah-U-Ekber." This was at Ovnak.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: From Ovnak, in the course of those battles, you were able to notice that four or five houses were on fire.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: Yes. I saw that as well as I see you now.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: However, you did not see who or how those houses had been set on fire.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BOHUTINSKI
utterances.text: No, I didn't see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Allow me now to refer to your statement given in November to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And to be able to ask the witness some questions, I would like him to be shown this statement. We have copies for the Trial Chamber and our learned friends. The Defence does not intend to tender this statement into evidence or to be marked for identification, but we would like to ask him some questions in relation to his testimony today.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm not sure if what Defence counsel -- could the statement be taken from the witness, please. Witness, could you please close that statement. I'm not sure -- as a matter of fact, I object to the course of action that Defence counsel is taking. Defence counsel may, if they wish to establish some previous inconsistent statement or for one or two other reasons, refer to the witness statement. But Defence counsel is not, it is my submission, entitled to put the statement in his hand and ask him whatever questions they want to ask him from the statement. So I think it would be useful if we begin by Defence counsel telling us what is the purpose of giving the witness a statement that he has already made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the Defence tell us what is the purpose of showing this statement to the witness. But we mustn't also forget the beginning, that originally this statement was suggested to be tendered into evidence by the Prosecution under 92 bis and it was the Defence who opposed it, and now the Defence is showing the document again. Now, what is the ultimate objective, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we are not presenting the statement to the Trial Chamber. We just wish to ask some questions regarding the knowledge of this witness about the structure of the army and his credibility we would like to check. Those are the reasons we are showing him this statement. Only two paragraphs from the statement and nothing more.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Respectfully -- respectfully, it is the submission of the Prosecution that the witness ought to be asked in examination, both in cross-examination and in examination-in-chief about matters that he can testify to without the assistance of documents. Only in certain circumstances, it is submitted, do the Rules allow him to be given a statement either to refresh his memory to contradict him with the previous inconsistent statement. But it would be improper for counsel to hand to any witness some previous statement they have given and generally just ask them questions about a previous statement. Perhaps counsel should ask the witness whatever they wish to ask the witness and there may be circumstances where it is permissible for them to hand to the witness a statement. That is my submission. May it please you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I should like to remind my learned friend, which he's aware of, that the position of the Appeals Chamber of this Tribunal is that a previous statement may be used, given under Rule 92 bis in the cross-examination, regardless of whether it was admitted or not. But that is not the latest decision. It has been the practice of this Tribunal and part of the Rules of the cross-examination. Let me put my first question to the witness, and then I will remind him of something that is stated in that statement. And I therefore think that the remarks of my learned friend are inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Anyhow, I think we're in agreement. So perhaps I could sit. She ought to put the questions to the witness and then in certain circumstances it might be permissible to use some document or previous statement of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. You put the question, and then you tell him, depending on the answer that you get, I'm showing you such and such a paragraph from your statement and what do you say to that? Rather than the reverse procedure. So put the question first, and then we will show him the relevant paragraphs. So as you have two questions only apparently - you mentioned two - what is your first question?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. In connection with two paragraphs in this statement. Maybe I wasn't quite specific enough.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
